title: Stay Under a Million
statement: For a positive integer $n$, call a subset $S$ of $\{1,2,\dots,n\}$, which may be empty, closed if both of the following hold: for every positive integer $k$ with $2k \le n$, we have $k \in S$ if and only if $2k \in S$; and for every positive integer $k$ with $3k \le n$, we have $k \in S$ if and only if $3k \in S$. What is the largest positive integer $n$ for which the number of closed subsets of $\{1,2,\dots,n\}$ is at most $1000000$?
hints: Take $n$ large and suppose $1 \in S$. Which other numbers are then forced into $S$? Which numbers are never affected by this choice, however large $n$ is?

Use prime factorisation to write each integer as $m \cdot 2^a \cdot 3^b$, where $m$ is coprime to $6$. Multiplying or dividing by $2$ or $3$ doesn't change $m$, so try grouping the numbers up to $n$ according to their value of $m$.

Numbers with the same $m$ must all be in $S$ or all be out of $S$, and different values of $m$ can be chosen independently. So the number of closed subsets is $2^c$, where $c$ is the number of integers from $1$ to $n$ coprime to $6$. Since $2^{19} \le 1000000 < 2^{20}$, we need $c \le 19$. Now list the integers coprime to $6$ in order and see where the count passes $19$.
solution:
Write each $x\le n$ uniquely as $m\cdot2^a3^b$ with $\gcd(m,6)=1$. The conditions say that $x$ and $2x$ (when $2x\le n$) have the same status, and likewise $x$ and $3x$ (when $3x\le n$). Multiplying by $2$ or $3$ preserves $m$, so the status is constant on each class of numbers with the same $m$. Conversely, any union of classes is closed.

Every class contains its $m$, since $m\le x\le n$, and $m$ is the only element coprime to $6$ in its class. So the number of classes is $c$, the number of integers in $[1,n]$ coprime to $6$, and there are $2^c$ closed sets.

Since $2^{19}=524288\le10^6<1048576=2^{20}$, we need $c\le19$. The integers coprime to $6$ are $1,5,7,11,13,17,19,23,25,29,31,35,37,41,43,47,49,53,55,59,\dots$, and the $20$th is $59$. Hence $c\le19$ exactly when $n\le58$.
